why.correct: Only a study that imposes the conditions, with chance deciding who gets which, supports cause and effect. Here the link may be due to confounding.
options: A large observational study still cannot rule out confounding variables.
A difference between groups that formed on their own can come from other differences between them.
Right: in an observational study the walkers may differ in other ways, such as age or diet, that affect blood pressure.
The measurement is fine; the problem is that walking was not imposed.

why.correct: A good investigative question names the population, the variable and the kind of answer (here a proportion), and can be answered with data that vary.
options: It is a survey item for one person, not a question about the population, and "like" is vague.
It asks about cause, which needs an experiment, and it does not name a population or a measurable variable.
Right: it names the population (Lincoln High students), the variable (phone use at lunch) and what to estimate (a proportion).
It has one answer about one student; there is no variation to study.

why.correct: The question is about every student at Lincoln High, so it asks for a parameter, the population proportion.
options: Right: the question is about the whole school, so it asks for a population proportion.
The council may estimate the answer with a statistic, but the question itself is about the whole school.
The question asks about use at lunch, not ownership.
The question asks for a proportion of students, not minutes.

why.correct: To estimate a proportion for a population, survey a sample chosen by chance from the whole population.
options: The council wants to know how students behave now, not the effect of a condition.
A census of 1,500 students’ phone records is impractical and private; a sample does the job.
Council members are not chosen to represent the school.
Right: asking a well chosen sample is practical and can estimate the school’s proportion.

why.correct: Questions about cause need an experiment. A survey or observational study shows only how variables are related.
options: Time is not the problem; the design of the study is.
Right: students who use phones may differ in other ways, so only an experiment that imposes phone use could show a cause.
They might answer; the issue is what the answers could show.
There is no such rule; the issue is cause and effect.

why.correct: A census gathers data from the entire population.
options: Right: a census measures the whole population, not a sample.
That describes an experiment.
That is a sample, and a poorly chosen one.
A census covers the whole population of interest, not one household.

why.correct: When the population is small and easy to reach, a census answers the question exactly.
options: A sample works, but with 28 students a census is easy and exact.
The teacher wants to know how long students slept, not the effect of a condition.
Right: the population is small, so measuring everyone is easy and gives the exact answer.
The question is about her own 28 students.

why.correct: Prospective: follow individuals forward and record outcomes. Retrospective: look back at existing records. Both are observational when nothing is imposed.
options: Retrospective studies look back at past records; this one looks forward.
Right: it follows people forward in time, recording what happens, without imposing anything.
Length does not matter. No diet is imposed, so it is observational.
The 5,000 adults are a sample of nonsmokers.

why.correct: A cause-and-effect question needs an experiment, in which the researcher imposes the conditions.
options: That describes a population; a sample survey answers it.
That is answered by measuring the plants as they are.
That asks about a relationship that already exists; an observational study answers it.
Right: a question about cause needs the researcher to impose the fertilizer on some plants and not others.

why.correct: An experiment deliberately imposes conditions on individuals to measure their responses; an observational study does not.
options: Observational studies also measure many variables.
Right: in an experiment the researcher decides who gets which condition.
Experiments can happen anywhere; what matters is imposing conditions.
Size does not decide the type of study.

why.correct: A confounding variable is related to both the explanatory and the response variables, so their effects on the response cannot be told apart.
options: Confounding is about variables mixing their effects, not about confusion.
That is a mixed effect, not confounding.
That is a concern about measurement, a different issue.
Right: if a third variable affects both, its effect is mixed up with breakfast’s.

why.correct: An investigative question names a population and a variable whose values vary, and asks for something data can estimate.
options: Right: it names a population and a variable that varies, and asks for a typical value.
One person, one answer: no variation to study.
A single fact to look up.
Too vague: no population, no measurable variable.

why.correct: A sample survey is an observational study: it records answers from a sample without imposing anything.
options: Right: a survey asks people about themselves without imposing any condition.
Answering questions is not a condition imposed to see a response.
A census asks every member of the population.
A survey shows relationships, not causes.

why.correct: Choosing n individuals so that every possible group of n has the same chance is a simple random sample.
options: Numbering the students is a step in choosing; nothing is split into strata.
Right: every group of 100 students has the same chance of being the sample.
A cluster sample takes whole groups such as homerooms; plan P picks individual students.
A systematic sample takes every kth individual after a random start.

why.correct: Splitting the population into strata and taking a simple random sample from each is a stratified random sample.
options: In a cluster sample whole groups are chosen and everyone in them is surveyed; plan Q samples within every grade.
Not every group of 100 is possible: a sample of 100 ninth graders cannot happen.
No every kth rule is used; students are chosen at random within each grade.
Right: the population is split into groups by grade and a simple random sample is taken from each.

why.correct: Choosing whole groups (clusters) at random and measuring every individual in them is cluster sampling. Its strength is convenience.
options: Right: clusters are chosen at random and everyone in them is included, which saves time.
Homerooms are chosen at random, so some grades may be missed; it is a cluster sample.
Each student does have the same chance, but not every group of 100 is possible, so it is not simple random.
The 4 homerooms are chosen at random, not by an every kth rule.

why.correct: Stratify by a variable that is related to the response: each stratum is represented, and estimates vary less from sample to sample.
options: Four random homerooms could all come from one or two grades.
A simple random sample could by chance include few students from some grade.
Right: stratifying by grade guarantees 25 students from each grade, and when grades differ it gives more precise results.
An alphabetical list has nothing to do with grade, so grades may be uneven.

why.correct: A systematic sample of every kth individual from N gives about <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>N</mi><mi>k</mi></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{N}{k}</annotation></semantics></math>: here <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1200</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1200}{12} = 100</annotation></semantics></math>.
options: 12 is the step size, not the sample size.
Only every 12th student is taken, not everyone after the start.

Right: taking every 12th student from a list of 1,200 gives <math class="stat-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mn>1200</mn><mn>12</mn></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>100</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{1200}{12} = 100</annotation></semantics></math> students.
Homerooms play no part in plan S.

why.correct: Label, generate random numbers, skip repeats, stop at 10 different labels, then measure those individuals.
A procedure must be clear enough that another person could carry it out exactly: label 1 to 80, generate, skip repeats, choose 10.
options: Right: someone else could not follow it. A procedure must label, generate, skip repeats and select.
A generator gives different numbers; the issue is the missing steps.
The sample size was set by time and equipment; the procedure is what is incomplete.
Either a table or a generator works when the steps are spelled out.

why.correct: Skipping repeats samples without replacement: each individual can be chosen once.
options: Skipping repeats is what prevents a pond from being chosen twice.
They can repeat numbers, which is exactly why the step is needed.
Skipping keeps the count at 10 different ponds.
Right: a pond already in the sample should not take a second place.

why.correct: The sampling frame is the list of individuals the sample is chosen from, here the map’s list of 80 ponds.
options: Those are the sample.
Right: the sampling frame is the list from which the sample is drawn.
That is the variable being measured.
Equipment is not a list of individuals.

why.correct: A simple random sample of size n gives every possible group of n individuals the same chance of being the sample.
options: Right: that is the definition. It is stronger than "each individual has the same chance".
Who arrives first is not chosen by chance.
That is what stratifying aims for; a simple random sample may miss a subgroup.
Choosing by judgment is not random.

why.correct: Stratify by groups whose members are similar to each other; cluster by groups that each resemble the whole population.
options: In stratified sampling every stratum is sampled; in cluster sampling clusters are chosen at random.
Size does not define them; what matters is how alike the individuals are within each group.
Right: strata group similar individuals; clusters work best when each one mixes the population.
They are used in opposite ways: sample within every stratum, or survey all of a few clusters.

why.correct: Systematic sampling is risky when the list has a pattern that repeats every k individuals.
options: Size is not the issue; the pattern in the list is.
Right: a systematic sample can land on the same kind of house every time if the list repeats with the same period.
A random start is exactly what makes it a systematic random sample.
Houses can be fine units; the trouble is choosing only one kind.

why.correct: With replacement, an individual can be selected more than once; a committee needs sampling without replacement.
options: A well mixed hat gives a random draw; the issue is putting names back.
Replacing names keeps chances the same on each draw, and allows repeats.
The size is a choice of the committee, not a sampling problem.
Right: for a committee of 3 different people, draw without replacement.

why.correct: A random sampling method uses chance to choose individuals: simple random, stratified, cluster and systematic with a random start.
options: Right: a simple random sample.
Right: a stratified random sample.
Who walks in first is not decided by chance.
Choosing by judgment is not random.

why.correct: When the population splits into groups that differ in the response, stratify by those groups.
options: One street is not chosen by chance and may differ from the rest of the city.
Right: spending likely differs by neighborhood, so stratifying gives each one its place and more precise results.
One cluster from a city of very different neighborhoods would represent the city poorly.
Choosing people you know is not random.

why.correct: A sampling frame is the list the sample is actually drawn from. Ideally it lists the whole population.
options: That is the sample size.
That is part of the survey, not the frame.
That is the schedule of the study.
Right: for example, a school roster or a list of addresses.

why.correct: When people choose whether to take part, the sample is a voluntary response sample.
options: In a convenience sample the researcher picks people who are easy to reach; here people pick themselves.
Right: people decide for themselves whether to answer.
No chance process chooses anyone.
No clusters are chosen at random; anyone who wants to can answer.

why.correct: Voluntary response samples overrepresent people with strong opinions, here most likely opponents of the fee, so the estimate is too high.
options: People with strong objections tend to respond most, which pushes the estimate up, not down.
Being able to answer is not the same as being chosen by chance; who answers is self-selected.
Many responses from a self-selected group are still biased.
Right: residents who feel strongly, often those angry about a new fee, are the most likely to bother answering.

why.correct: Choosing whoever is easy to reach gives a convenience sample. Downtown shoppers, many of whom drive and park there, may differ from other residents.
options: Right: shoppers on one street on a weekday afternoon are easy to reach but may differ from residents as a whole.
The interviewers choose whom to approach; people do not sign themselves up.
Downtown drivers are likely overrepresented, not left out.
Plan 2 uses interviews, not mail.

why.correct: Nonresponse occurs when individuals chosen for the sample cannot be reached or do not respond.
options: Undercoverage is about people left out of the frame; these 500 were chosen, then 290 did not reply.
The sample was chosen at random; the problem is that many chosen people did not answer.
Right: people chosen for the sample did not respond, and they may differ from those who did.
Response bias is about answers that are not truthful; here there are no answers from 290 people.

why.correct: When the sampling frame misses part of the population, those individuals have no chance of being chosen: undercoverage.
options: Nonresponse is a separate problem in plan 3; the frame itself causes undercoverage.
People register to vote, not to be in a survey; the issue is who the list leaves out.
Right: the frame leaves part of the population out, and those residents may feel differently about the fee.
People who register are not chosen by chance and may differ from those who do not.

why.correct: Question wording that leads people toward an answer causes response bias.
options: Right: the wording pushes people toward an answer, so the answers do not reflect their true views.
Wording does not leave anyone out of the sampling frame.
People can answer either version; the problem is how the wording shapes the answers.
That is about how people are chosen, not how they are asked.

why.correct: Loaded words such as "small" and "clean and safe" push answers toward yes; "new tax" pushes them toward no.
options: "Tax" usually makes people less willing, not more.
Clearer, perhaps, but "tax on drivers" tends to raise opposition.
Wording is one of the best known causes of response bias.
Right: the wording frames the fee as minor and beneficial.

why.correct: A neutral question describes the issue plainly, without loaded words, and offers both sides.
options: It suggests a benefit and asks people to agree.
Right: it states the fee plainly and gives both sides.
"Forced" and "yet another" push toward no.
Telling people what others think pressures them to agree.

why.correct: A larger sample does not fix bias. Only changing the method (neutral wording) does.
options: Right: bias is built into the method, so a bigger sample just gives a more confident wrong answer.
Sample size reduces chance variation, not bias.
Random sampling handles who is chosen, not how they are asked.
More people hearing the same loaded question still lean the same way.

why.correct: A biased method systematically favors some outcomes, so its estimates are off in the same direction again and again.
options: Chance variation from sample to sample is expected even in a good method; bias is a consistent push one way.
Bias in statistics is about the method, not the researcher’s feelings.
Right: bias is a systematic error that repeats sample after sample.
Every sample is smaller than its population; that alone is not bias.

why.correct: A voluntary response sample is biased toward people with strong views. A huge sample does not fix it.
options: Size is not the issue; who chose to respond is.
Right: a voluntary response sample is biased however large it is.
There is no such rule; the problem is self-selection.
A high percent is possible; the method is what makes it untrustworthy.

why.correct: Undercoverage happens when the sampling frame leaves out part of the population, here people without landlines.
options: They are in the frame and likely to respond.
Having a phone at home puts people in the frame, not outside it.
Refusing after being chosen is nonresponse, not undercoverage.
Right: people with no landline are missing from the frame, and they tend to be younger.

why.correct: Sensitive questions, especially asked in person, cause response bias: the proportion who admit cheating will likely be too low.
options: Absence is possible, but the main problem is untruthful answers.
Right: a sensitive question asked in person invites untruthful answers, which underestimates cheating.
Every student is on the list; the issue is honesty.
The teacher asks each student; the problem is how they answer.

why.correct: Explain bias by the method: a nonrandom sample may differ systematically from the population. Name how it differs and the likely direction.
options: That would be a calculation error, not a problem with the sample.
Convenience samples are fast; that is their appeal.
Any sample can give a percent; size is not what makes it biased.
Right: the issue is that the method is not random, not the sample size.

why.correct: Nonresponse is a chosen individual who cannot be reached or will not answer.
options: Right: chosen individuals could not be reached.
That is undercoverage: those people were never in the frame.
That leading wording causes response bias.
That is a voluntary response sample.

why.correct: Random sampling from a complete frame prevents selection bias. Nonresponse and response bias can still happen after people are chosen.
options: Right: random selection removes selection bias, but chosen people can still fail to answer or answer untruthfully.
People were chosen by chance, not self-selected.
Chance chose the sample, not convenience.
The list is complete, so no adult is left out.

why.correct: Experimental units are the individuals to which treatments are assigned: here the 60 students.
options: The glasses are the treatments.
Right: the units are the individuals the treatments are given to.
The scores are the response.
The trackers measure the response; they are not what the treatments are applied to.

why.correct: A treatment is a condition imposed on the units; the response variable is what is measured afterward.
options: The students are the experimental units; the glasses are imposed on them.
This reverses them: the glasses are imposed, and sleep is measured.
The trackers record the response, sleep quality.
Right: the researcher imposes the glasses and measures sleep quality.

why.correct: A placebo control group receives a fake treatment, so the placebo effect is the same in both groups and the comparison isolates the real effect.
options: Right: any effect of simply wearing glasses, or of expecting better sleep, shows up in both groups.
Cost is not the reason; the clear glasses control for the placebo effect.
The glasses do not set how long students sleep.
The glasses are assigned at random, not chosen.

why.correct: When neither the subjects nor those who interact with them or measure the response know who received which treatment, the experiment is double-blind.
options: Single-blind means one side, usually the subjects, does not know; here both sides are kept in the dark.
Matched pairs is about pairing units, not about who knows the treatments.
Right: both the subjects and the person measuring the response are blind to the treatments.
The treatments are imposed, so this is an experiment.

why.correct: Random assignment balances other variables between groups on average, so a large difference in the response supports a cause-and-effect conclusion, for units like these.
options: Generalizing needs a random sample from a population; these are volunteers.
An experiment compares groups; it does not promise an effect for each person.
Right: chance made the groups similar in every other way, on average, so a large difference can be traced to the treatment.
Random assignment makes groups similar on average, not identical.

why.correct: Grouping similar units into blocks and randomizing treatments within each block is a randomized block design.
options: Right: members are grouped by experience into blocks, and treatments are assigned at random within each block.
In a completely randomized design all 40 members would be assigned in one draw, without grouping first.
Matched pairs uses pairs of similar units, or each unit receives both treatments.
Stratifying is for choosing a sample; blocking is for assigning treatments in an experiment.

why.correct: Block on a variable that is expected to affect the response. Comparing treatments within blocks keeps that variable from hiding the treatment effect.
options: Both programs are given within each block; that is the point.
The blocks have different sizes, 16 and 24; that is fine.
Blocking is a statistical choice, not a social one.
Right: blocking accounts for a known source of variation and makes the comparison of programs more precise.

why.correct: Label (identical slips), mix, draw 8 for P, and the rest get Q. Then repeat the process for the experienced block.
Random assignment supports cause and effect; without random sampling, the conclusion applies to units like those in the experiment.
options: The members were volunteers, not a random sample of all gym members.
Right: random assignment supports cause and effect, but the units are volunteers from one gym, which limits generalizing.
With random assignment, a cause-and-effect conclusion is justified.
Unequal block sizes are fine; each block is randomized on its own.

why.correct: Matched pairs: each unit (or each pair of similar units) receives both treatments, with the order or side decided at random.
options: Right: each volunteer receives both treatments, one per arm, with chance deciding which arm gets which.
Here each volunteer gets both sunscreens, one per arm; one sunscreen per volunteer would be a completely randomized design.
The sunscreens are imposed, so this is an experiment.
This is about assigning treatments, not sampling.

why.correct: Replication means using enough experimental units in each treatment group so that chance variation between units averages out.
options: Repeating a whole study is useful, but in design, replication means many units per treatment.
Repeated measurement is a different idea.
Right: with many units per treatment, chance differences between units tend to even out.
An experiment compares two or more treatments.

why.correct: A statistically significant difference is larger than what chance variation in the random assignment would usually produce.
options: Statistically significant is about chance, not about practical size.
Right: random assignment by itself would rarely create a difference this big.
Statistics gives evidence, not proof, and effects vary between individuals.
Precision of measurement is a separate issue.

why.correct: In a completely randomized design, every unit is assigned to a treatment by chance, with no grouping first.
options: Choosing by height confounds height with fertilizer.
Choice by a person can favor one fertilizer.
That is a randomized block design.
Right: every plant is assigned by chance, with no blocks.

why.correct: A control group (no treatment, a placebo, or the current standard) shows what happens without the new treatment, so the comparison isolates its effect.
options: A control group gets no treatment, a placebo or the standard treatment.
Right: without a comparison group, improvements could come from time, attention or the placebo effect.
A control group adds subjects; it does not reduce them.
That is blinding, which is related but different.

why.correct: When subjects choose their own treatment, other differences between them (such as motivation) are confounded with the treatment. Random assignment prevents this.
options: Cost does not affect what the comparison shows.
A quantitative response is fine.
Many students is good for replication.
Right: without random assignment, motivation is mixed up with the effect of the tool.

why.correct: The placebo effect is a response to a fake treatment, driven by expectation. A placebo control group lets researchers measure the real treatment against it.
options: Right: expecting to feel better can change how people feel.
Response bias is about untrue survey answers; here the improvement is in how patients feel.
Replication is about many units per treatment.
The pill has no active ingredient; the effect comes from expectation.

why.correct: Random assignment is what supports cause and effect. Random sampling is what supports generalizing to a population.
options: Right: it balances other variables between groups, on average.
That allows generalizing to the population, not a causal conclusion.
Size helps replication, but volunteers who choose treatments still allow confounding.
Measuring more variables does not remove confounding.

why.correct: Random assignment supports cause and effect; random sampling supports generalizing. This study had the first but not the second.
